description: We’re a Ukrainian team brought together by astrophysics and software. Our project grew out of a simple question. If you look at the same patch of sky twice, what has moved? We built SPHEREx Time Lab so anyone with a browser can look for an answer in real telescope images, even if they’ve never opened an astronomy archive before.
summary:
What changes when a telescope looks at the same patch of sky months later? SPHEREx Time Lab is a free web tool that lets anyone explore that question with real infrared images from NASA’s SPHEREx mission.

Choose any location on the sky by clicking the map or entering its coordinates. You can start with Barnard’s Star, one of the challenge’s suggested targets, or explore a field around any of the millions of other objects in the survey. Where repeat observations are available, play them in order or compare two dates side by side. If something catches your eye, share a link to the field so someone else can take a look.
details:
We started with a simple task: choose a patch of sky, find out when SPHEREx observed it, and compare those observations. In SPHEREx Time Lab, you can click a location on the sky map or enter its coordinates. The lab searches the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive for individual exposures, aligns their cutouts to a common sky grid, and puts them in time order. You can play the sequence, view two exposures side by side, or blink between them.

Barnard’s Star illustrates why the dates matter. Its position changes relative to more distant stars, so the lab uses its cataloged motion to center the archive search. The search also includes the other four targets named in the challenge: Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis. A prepared SPHEREx Data Release 1 field lets visitors try the comparison tools with observations from August 2025 and February 2026.

When something looks different, you can inspect the observation time, wavelength, and quality flags, then follow the link to the original archive record. The lab can also overlay Gaia DR3 catalog positions for the observation date. These checks matter because a change in wavelength or flagged pixels can affect what you see in an image.
